```json
{
  "winner": "A",
  "reasons": [
    "Idea A has stronger evidence that people pay, which matters most for getting a first customer within 90 days. Grapevine charges a flat $25/month and has 223 reviews at 5.0. Fairing publishes tiers from $49 to $149. A sourced Indie Hackers post describes a solo founder reaching $125K MRR on this exact problem. Idea B's competitors are mostly free, in beta, waitlist-only or unpriced. Only apidrift ($29/mo) and Nalvis ($14/mo) publish prices, and neither brief shows that anyone actually pays them.",
    "Idea B's demand evidence (three dev.to and Reddit quotes) shows the pain is real. None of it shows willingness to pay. Idea A's Reddit merchant at least shows a manual workaround that failed, which points toward wanting an automated tool.",
    "Idea A's buyer is easier to sell to. Idea B needs PR-opening access to customer source code. The brief flags this as trust-sensitive, along with security reviews and about 8x false-positive over-reporting on raw spec diffs. That is a hard first sale for an unknown solo operator. Idea A also has data-trust hurdles (GDPR, DPA, store data access), but the brief frames them as a one-time legal review plus building reviews over time.",
    "Both ideas are crowded, with six competitors each and free tiers in both. So crowding does not separate them. What separates them is that A's crowding comes with proof of a paying market, while B's crowding comes with a free-to-beta pricing floor and no revenue evidence.",
    "The Shopify App Store is an established self-serve marketplace with demonstrated paying merchants. B's GitHub Marketplace channel is described only in terms of setup cost, with no evidence of buyer conversion."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "Idea B's community-channel economics rest on a $248 median devtools CAC with a 9.4-month payback. The brief itself notes the source page contained a prompt-injection attempt and should be treated as directional only, so I treat it as effectively missing. Close behind is the price hypothesis, anchored on apidrift's $29/mo list price with no evidence of a single paying apidrift customer.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate to low. Both briefs describe saturated niches with free incumbents. Idea A's own brief undercuts it on the 90-day timeline: its poster child, Zigpoll, took two years to gain traction despite an experienced founder, and a zero-review app may struggle to convert installs to paid. A wins mainly because its market shows verifiable paying customers and B's does not. It does not win because A has a clear path to beating its incumbents."
}
```
